The Social Security COLA for 2027 is set. Here's what experts say you need to know
Economy
Updated on Oct 14, 2026 8:56 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 14, 2026 6:31 PM EDT
Social Security checks will increase by roughly $76 per month for the average retired worker in 2027, the federal government announced Wednesday.
The payment jump is due to the Social Security Administration's annual COLA, or cost-of-living adjustment, which has been determined each fall for decades. Next year's increase is 3.6%, based on inflation data, amounting to a little more than $900 next year.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
"The COLA is really one of the only things in most people's retirement portfolios that is inflation-adjusted," said Bill Sweeney, senior vice president for government affairs at AARP. "That really means that Social Security becomes an increasingly important part of your retirement portfolio as you get older."
People 62 or older and those with a disability or blindness can receive Social Security benefits. Some dependents or surviving spouses of people who have died can also collect payments.
Here's what experts say Social Security beneficiaries need to know about the cost-of-living adjustment for 2027.
What is the COLA and how is it calculated?
Next year's cost-of-living adjustment of 3.6% is the highest since 2023, when payments increased 8.7% from the prior year's already higher 5.9% jump.
The COLA is a mathematical formula tied to consumer prices. For more than 50 years, Social Security beneficiaries have gotten annual adjustments to keep up with inflation. If inflation is low, so too are COLAs, but when inflation spikes, as it has on-and-off for the past six years, the COLAs can be big jumps.
Next year's adjustment is "not wildly outside of the norm," said Shai Akabas, vice president for economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center. Because inflation has remained above the Federal Reserve's target of 2% year over year since 2021, COLAs have generally also been higher than that, he said.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics calculates the adjustment by finding the percent change between the average consumer price index for workers for July through September of the current year and the same figure for the previous year. If the percent change is negative, there's no adjustment for the following year.
Because inflation has been so volatile sector by sector, it may be hard to predict what a COLA will feel like when it takes effect in January, Akabas said.
But the adjustment isn't necessarily meant to be a perfect fix.
"It's meant to be as close to an approximation and current a measure as can be done," Akabas said, that then "needs to be incorporated into millions and millions of benefit payments and be communicated throughout the system."
What does next year's COLA mean for people who receive Social Security?
The 3.6% increase is "a significant amount of money," Sweeney said. But with rising costs, it can still be hard for consumers to keep up, he said.
READ MORE: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% as midterm elections near
An AARP poll of some 1,000 adults aged 50 and older found that 76% of respondents said a projected increase of 3.5% would not be enough to keep up with rising prices. That includes 80% of Social Security recipients.
Instead, about 7 in 10 of older adults said an increase between 5% and 8% would be "sufficient" to help Social Security recipients afford expenses — a number that has remained relatively consistent over the past three years AARP has conducted its poll.
Over time, older Americans lose buying power, said Mary Johnson, an independent Social Security and Medicare policy analyst who receives benefits herself.
That's partly because older adults spend more on healthcare than younger adults, while the COLA is based on the costs of urban wage earners, which does not include retired people. People 65 and older spent nearly 2.5 times the amount working-age people spent on healthcare in 2020, according to the government.
Next year's COLA may also be undercut by a rise in Medicare Part B premiums, which wasn't the case when Social Security recipients got a huge COLA in 2023. That could take a bite out of people's COLA increases, Akabas said, though recent estimates put premium increases at probably less than $20 per month, he added.
The effect of the Social Security payment increase will also vary from household to household, Akabas said. Gas has remained particularly elevated recently, he added, so the COLA may overcompensate for people who use less gas and be insufficient for those who fill up more frequently.
Even within the older population, there's spending nuance, Akabas said.
When Johnson tracked her own budget in 2025 and 2026, for example, she saw spending spikes that exceeded 3.5% in every category, including medical and dental insurance, electricity, groceries and property taxes.
There's debate on how and whether the Social Security Administration should change its formula for calculating COLAs, but a perfect solution may be elusive.
"It's difficult to create one cost-of-living index that applies to everybody in a group as diverse and large as Social Security beneficiaries," Akabas said.

Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
World
Oct 17, 2026 12:28 PM EDT
JERUSALEM (AP) — Masked settlers attacked a group of European diplomats during a visit to the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister said, on a second day of high-profile assaults on Palestinians and others during the sensitive olive harvest.
READ MORE: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during West Bank olive harvest and beat U.S. photojournalist
At least four people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. Activists say Israeli authorities do little to stop attacks that involve weapons ranging from slingshots to guns. An attack on Friday seriously injured a Washington Post photographer and others.
In Saturday's attack in the village of Taybeh, settlers targeted Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives, Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said.
"A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team is safe," Prevot said. He linked the attack to what he called Israel's "illegal settlement policy" and pledged to push for further European Union sanctions.
Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians as the "occupying power," Prevot added. "Impunity for violent settlers must end."
The attacks came less than two weeks before closely contested elections that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's time in office. His government, the most nationalist and far-right in Israel's history, faces domestic criticism over security failures and international criticism over the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza.
Israel's military called Saturday's attack on the diplomats a "severe act of violence," but said the visit had not been coordinated with it and no soldiers were at the scene.
Israeli police said they had opened an investigation.
"The Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will work to complete these investigations until everyone who took part in these cases is brought to justice," the police statement said.
"I strongly condemn the severe acts of violence by Israeli rioters," Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said on X, adding that his ministry was in contact with ambassadors from the countries concerned.

House Speaker Mike Johnson draws on faith as he fights to hold the Republican majority
Politics
Oct 17, 2026 12:17 PM EDT
BANGOR, Maine (AP) — Ever the optimist, Speaker Mike Johnson said he believes Republicans will hold on to their U.S. House majority, defying a surge of Democratic momentum in the final stretch of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.
It's the crowds he says he's seeing as he crosses the country campaigning for GOP candidates. The caliber of recruits and incumbents he calls workhorses, not show horses. And the nearly half a billion he has raised for House Republicans.
He also has faith.
"We run to win, and that's biblical: You run to win," he told The Associated Press during a campaign stop in Maine.
"And I believe that we will."
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
The speaker of the House is one of the most consequential elected officials in the United States, second in line of succession to the president. While Johnson quipped to Fox News recently that he may return to his hometown of Shreveport, Louisiana, to start a lawn care business if Republicans lose power on Nov. 3, he fully expects to buck an American midterm tradition that often sees the president's party dumped in Congress.
It can be said that Johnson, who has drawn so close to President Donald Trump that he routinely fields 1 a.m. calls — they spoke the night before as Trump rallied in Alaska — walks on the sunny side of the street. That's despite voter frustration over high prices and the Iran war, and his own challenge of leading one of narrowest House majorities in modern times.
In his three years as speaker, Johnson has pushed past the doubters and naysayers, holding his thread-thin GOP majority together to deliver Trump's agenda. He notably led passage of the big tax breaks and social service cuts bill. Most days he does not have a single vote to spare.
WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists on how Trump's unpopularity is shaping the midterms
"So many times everybody had written off, there was no way he was going to be able to pull off a particular vote," said Republican Rep. Mark Harris of North Carolina, who joined the speaker on the campaign swing. "Yet he always seems to pull out the win in the end."
In the interview, Johnson did not speak brashly about expanding the House majority on Election Day, as he has in the past. But on track to visit more than 20 states and 40 congressional districts though November, he said the political mood reminds him of the 2024 election that swept Republicans to control of Congress and the White House.
"It's not going to be a giant majority," he said. "But I genuinely believe that we will have a working majority."
Accidental speaker becomes emboldened by Trump
Johnson first fell into the speaker's job almost by accident, a desperate choice by his GOP colleagues after a contingent of renegade Republicans ousted his predecessor, -then-Rep. Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., in 2023.
Johnson had been a lower-level member of House leadership, but distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump's false claims of widespread fraud in the election that he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
In the time since, Johnson has secured proximity to Trump's power. He joined Trump at a UFC fight in New York and once gifted the president a speaker's gavel as Trump signed the "One Big Beautiful Bill" into law. It was a symbolic act, but one that critics saw as giving away the authority of a coequal branch of government.
READ MORE: Republicans retreat from battleground districts as lines shift in House races
More recently, Johnson abruptly sent lawmakers home early rather than face a vote forced by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as lawmakers tried to halt the Iran war, which has not been authorized by Congress.
Over coffee in Bangor, after rallying for House candidate Paul LePage, a former governor, Johnson brushed back criticism that Congress has eroded under his watch as Trump works to amass executive power.
"Absolute nonsense," Johnson said.
"We did not yield Article One authority to the president," referring to the powers spelled out in the Constitution. "We used our own," he said, to muscle GOP priorities past Democratic opposition.
As House majority teeters, Trump's agenda is at risk
Johnson has focused the election on Democrats he portrays as "communists." A handful of far-left liberals, backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, are on the ballot.
U.S. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House Democratic leader who is in line for the speaker's gavel if his party sweeps to power, is preparing a first-100 days agenda for when the new Congress convenes in January, if there is a change in control.
What the Republicans will do if they retain power is less defined.
READ MORE: 5 House districts where Republicans are looking to turn the tables as Democrats eye big midterm wins
"Lots of plans," Johnson said, "along the same course of what we've been doing — less taxes, less regulation."
Trump "wants to go big for his legacy," he said. "We have big things on the horizon that we can do."

Trump's decision to waive Russian sanctions outrages Congress, but no quick counter seen
Politics
Oct 17, 2026 11:57 AM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's abrupt decision to waive sanctions on Russia days before they were to take effect drew outrage Saturday from members of Congress, which had overwhelmingly passed the legislation in a bipartisan display of American support for Ukraine in the war with Russia.
Lawmakers from both parties blasted the executive order late Friday, the latest in a series of steps that the Republican president has taken drawing the United States closer to Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump recently announced a diesel deal with Putin to import Russian energy in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices in the U.S. that are roiling the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
"Beyond irresponsible," said Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., on social media, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed hope that the sanctions that were supposed to take effect Sunday targeting Russian's economy could be revived.
"What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Tillis said. "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine."
Tillis said that if Trump wants to actually bring down energy prices, he should resolve the Iran war, which is largely blamed for the spike at the pump, and "not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."
Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas said "Lindsey would be appalled," referring to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., who worked endlessly on the bill before he died this summer. The bill is known as the Lindsey Graham Russian Sanctions Act.
READ MORE: Trump's diesel deal with Putin draws bipartisan criticism from a frustrated Congress
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a statement that "by giving the Russian economy life support, Trump's deal with the devil keeps getting dirtier."
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said Trump is "thumbing his nose" at Congress and "enabling Vladimir Putin to continue his war of aggression." She urged her colleagues to take action to reverse course.
Trump's actions come as Ukraine is bracing for a stark winter confronting Russia's ongoing attacks on its energy infrastructure to heat homes and keep the lights on. Zelenskyy, who has endured a rocky relationship with Trump but stayed close to the U.S. lawmakers, urged supporters to speak out on behalf of the sanctions.
The next steps are highly uncertain with the House and Senate are on recess until after Election Day. Trump said he was waiving the sanctions indefinitely, citing national security concerns. It is unlikely Congress would be in a position to take any action to challenge Trump's moves until lawmakers return to Washington.
Skeptics in Congress warned Trump would not follow the law
It took almost a year for Graham to persuade Trump to agree to the Russian sanctions package. It was designed to impose steep tariffs on countries that import large amounts of Russian oil and energy products and was promoted as way to halt the flow of funds fueling Putin's four-year war against Ukraine.
But even as Zelenskyy had watched from the visitor gallery as the Senate advanced the package after Graham's death, skeptics in Congress warned Trump would be unlikely to follow the bill once he had signed it into law a month ago.
READ MORE: Kremlin relishes in U.S.-Russia diesel deal and Trump's criticism of Zelenskyy
Last week, a bipartisan group of senators urged the Trump administration to more quickly clamp down on Russia, particularly the "shadow fleet" of tankers that Moscow is using to transport oil and bypass America's sanctions. The senators noted that the bulk of the new law's provisions were to be effective Sunday.
Instead, Trump soon announced the diesel deal with Putin, saying that Russia had agreed to supply tons of fuel to the U.S., where gas prices have skyrocketed in some areas and voters saying affordability issues are a top concern.
Outraged lawmakers have pledged to stop the Trump-Putin deal.
New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee who had led opposition to the Graham bill — warning that Trump would flout the law — introduced legislation Friday that would block Trump's diesel deal with Putin. "At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine," Meeks said in a statement.
He called the deal "corrupt" and said it "goes against everything the United States stands for."
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking and Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report.

Pope returns to Vatican days after surgery; surgeon says he should be fit for Latin America tour
World
Updated on Oct 17, 2026 1:21 PM EDT — Published on
Oct 17, 2026 11:27 AM EDT
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV's cancer surgeon said there are "no clinical reasons" to prevent the pontiff's planned Latin America trip next month, as the pope returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after undergoing lung surgery.
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."
WATCH: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer and prognosis
Leo, 71, is scheduled to make an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
"As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," Margaritora said.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
Pope says he feels 'much better'
"I am much better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV.
Leo greeted patients inside the hospital alongside his surgeon, before waving to well-wishers outside who cried out "Holiness" as he walked to a waiting vehicle.
He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter's Square last December—an encounter she told reporters "gave her the strength to overcome the illness."
READ MORE: What is adenocarcinoma? Here's what to know about Pope Leo XIV's form of lung cancer
Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
He will take on his first official duty on Sunday, delivering the traditional Angelus blessing to the faithful in St. Peter's Square. It comes exactly one week after the pontiff revealed to throngs in the square that the nodule had been found and would be surgically removed — an unusually candid revelation for the Vatican.
Further tests being carried out
Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital, also confirmed that the nodule was discovered by chance during routine abdominal examinations. It appeared as "a small spot" at the base of the lung, which extends down to the diaphragm, he said.
He added that if the spot had been higher up, "it certainly would not have been seen."
The cancer was in its early stages, and the pope had "no respiratory symptoms, and felt perfectly well," Margaritora said.
He described Tuesday's procedure to remove the lobe as "routine" and "without complications," but acknowledged that it "stirred deep feelings ... to operate on a pope, who for the first time – at least in modern history – is undergoing surgery for a malignant tumor."
READ MORE: South Americans pray for Pope Leo's recovery as uncertainty hangs over his visit
The Vatican did not disclose that the tumor was malignant until after Tuesday's successful surgery. It later confirmed that the pope had undergone a biopsy before being admitted to Gemelli. Experts say the Ion robotic bronchoscopy would have indicated whether the tumor was malignant and possibly whether cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.
Margaritora said the pope's recovery so far had required "very little assistance from us."
"His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect. It was truly commendable," the surgeon said.

Fundraising to protect key natural sites falls short ahead of UN biodiversity summit
World
Oct 16, 2026 7:58 PM EDT
Efforts to raise hundreds of billions of dollars to preserve the world's oceans, forests, rivers, lakes and other parts of the natural world have fallen short ahead of a key U.N. summit on biodiversity.
The yawning gap between the stated ambition of nations to protect biodiversity and what money has been raised will be a central topic in Yerevan, Armenia, when the biodiversity conference, known as COP17, gets started on Monday. The nearly two-week event, scheduled to end Oct. 30, is a chance for nearly 200 countries that are part of the treaty to take stock of their progress on 23 global targets after agreeing to a historic deal crafted in Montreal in 2022. The United States is not a party to the treaty.
Countries in Montreal committed to protect 30% of land and water considered important for biodiversity by 2030, a goal known as 30x30.
READ MORE: UN biodiversity talks end with nations backing $200 billion per year plan to protect nature
They also promised to raise $200 billion a year by 2030 for biodiversity and begin phasing out or reforming subsidies that could provide another $500 billion for nature. There were also commitments to increase to $20 billion annually by 2025 money that went to poor countries. That number would increase to $30 billion each year by 2030.
"We're not moving fast enough," convention executive secretary Astrid Schomaker told The Associated Press, before a U.N. progress report released Thursday found fewer than half of parties' biodiversity targets are on track and that current commitments would only protect 26% of land and only 12% of sea by 2030.
Data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development showed countries were raising between $75 billion and $92 billion each year from 2023 to 2025 — less than half the 2030 goal. Commitments to reduce $500 billion in harmful subsidies — government support and funding for sectors like fisheries and agriculture — have gained little traction, with few countries identifying which subsidies they would cut.
Countries were on track to provide the $20 billion to poor countries by 2025. The latest data showed $19 billion had been raised in 2024. But a drop in foreign aid raises questions over whether the upward trend will continue.
"Do we have enough money actually to finance the commitments that countries have made? And how do we get more finance to flow toward biodiversity positive outcomes?" Schomaker said. "That is the crucial question for the COP."
Biodiversity has taken a beating worldwide
The campaign to protect biodiversity, which first garnered global attention with the Rio Earth Summit in 1992, has often seemed like a losing battle.
In a bid to grow their economies and support increasing populations, countries have converted forests into farm land, overfished their waters and reduced habitats of many plants and animals through unchecked development. Climate change, at the same time, has created the conditions for widespread wildfires and prolonged droughts that have decimated ecosystems.
As a result, three-quarters of the world's land has been "severely altered" by humans and a million of the world's plants and animals are threatened with extinction, according to a 2019 U.N. report. Wildlife populations have also plummeted, according to the WWF's 2026 Living Planet Report released this month. They have declined on average by 73% between 1970 and 2022.
"We are losing everything that matters for us as humans on this planet," Schomaker said.
Meanwhile, there are some signs that countries are protecting more biodiversity. Countries have announced over 5,000 initiatives tied to the treaty.
A report from the Campaign for Nature, a global initiative which has spearheaded the 30x30 effort, found that countries in Latin America have already committed to protecting 29% of their land while those in Oceania have promised to preserve 41% of their seas. Last year, the Philippines created a marine protected area where catching rays and sharks is prohibited, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society. In 2023, Cambodia set aside almost 100,000 acres (40,000 hectares) of flooded grassland habitat for protection while Argentina created a national park in 2024.
At the conference on Friday, a 17-nation coalition was launched to accelerate species recovery. It also would support one of the Convention targets, which calls for halting extinction of threatened species and reducing extinction risk. Nine private organizations, including the Bezos Earth Fund, also announced plans to spend $500 million over the next five years to prevent extinctions and recover the world's most threatened species.
"We have a shared responsibility to ensure that threatened species have a future," said Fabio Alberto Arjona Hincapié, Colombia's minister of environment and sustainable development, whose country is a coalition co-chair.
Brian O'Donnell, director of the Campaign for Nature, said where and what we need to protect is clear, as are the methods to do so.
"What is now needed is an upswing in political ambition and determination," said O'Donnell.
O'Donnell said an international agreement reached last year to protect marine diversity on the high seas — the High Seas Treaty — would help

Israeli settlers attack Palestinians during West Bank olive harvest and beat U.S. photojournalist
World
Oct 16, 2026 7:46 PM EDT
ABU FALAH, West Bank (AP) — Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian villages across the occupied West Bank on Friday, setting fire to cars and trees and beating residents and a foreign journalist, in the latest violence to disrupt the territory's annual olive harvest this month.
Local officials and the Palestine Red Crescent Society reported attacks in at least eight villages in the northern West Bank, where most of the olive groves are concentrated and tens of thousands of Palestinian families depend on them for income.
Settler violence against Palestinians has soared this year and spiked further in the weeks leading up to Israel's election on Oct. 27. The far-right government that has emboldened the settlers could soon be voted out of power — or win another term.
Israeli authorities have done little to stop the attacks, according to residents and rights groups, who say the military has aided, protected or stood by as settlers lay siege to Palestinian villages. The violence has drawn accusations of " ethnic cleansing " — including from the British government, which has said Israel is turning a "blind eye" to the campaign underway.
"Soldiers aren't stopping the violence or protecting Palestinians," said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Israeli rights group Yesh Din. "If anything, they're sometimes assisting settlers in the attacks."
Journalist attacked while covering harvest
The West Bank has been under Israeli military rule since the 1967 Mideast war and today is home to around 3 million Palestinians and more than 500,000 Israeli settlers. The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said last month that more than 1,600 attacks across the territory had been reported between January and August. Yesh Din and other rights groups say authorities rarely arrest or indict the perpetrators.
Israel's military on Friday condemned the violence and acknowledged that a journalist was injured in Abu Falah.
On Friday, settlers attacked the village as residents, accompanied by peace activists, set out early for the harvest.
As the group of masked vigilantes approached, several members beat Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was hospitalized for her injuries.
The perpetrators — armed with bottles and slingshots — "were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag," Levine said.
Levine said her helmet and protective vest, which was marked "PRESS," likely saved her from more serious injuries.
Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post, speaks to journalists at the hospital after sustaining multiple injuries during an attack by Israeli militant settlers on Palestinians harvesting olives, in Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, Oct. 16, 2026. Photo by Ali Sawafta/Reuters
Both the Washington Post and the Foreign Press Association, which represents international journalists working in Israel and the Palestinian territories, called on Israel to bring the attackers to justice.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," the Foreign Press Association said.
WATCH: Violence surges in West Bank as Israeli settlers escalate attacks on Palestinians
The U.S. State Department said that "we condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," adding that it has reached out to The Washington Post to offer consular assistance.
Israeli troops later arrived in Abu Falah and drove up to the village after dispersing the crowd in the olive groves. Residents said that soldiers later fired live ammunition at village council member Abdel Jaber Hassan, even though he was unarmed and far from the trees. The military said that soldiers had fired because an individual was running toward them with a sharp object.
Nazem Saleh Shoman, another village council member, denied that account and said Hassan was shot at close range while carrying olive harvesting tools.
Across the West Bank, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said that its medics had tended to 14 wounded people in six locations, while local officials reported at least four injuries in two additional villages.
'Nothing has been left intact'
At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured since harvest season began earlier this month, the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry said last week. Yesh Din said on Friday that it had already documented hundreds of incidents of settler violence directly related to this year's harvest.
In Turmus Ayya, a village northeast of Ramallah, mayor Nawaf Zghoul said settlers early Friday had burned several cars in the hamlet's surrounding olive groves.
"The settlers were lying in wait for farmers working on their land and attacked them," he said. "Nothing has been left intact."
Israel's military said that suspects had fled the scene before troops arrived.

DOJ says California officials who process ballots from suspected noncitizens risk prosecution
Politics
Oct 16, 2026 7:30 PM EDT
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is escalating its fight with California ahead of next month's midterm election, warning that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
READ MORE: Trump administration sues California to block counting of alleged noncitizen mail ballots
The letter Friday from a senior Justice Department official and obtained first by The Associated Press is the latest salvo in an ongoing tussle with heavily Democratic California, coming just a day after the Trump administration sued the state to prevent it from counting mail ballots from people the federal government has identified as "likely" noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
"The legal consequences for either facilitating or ignoring a federal crime are significant. Noncitizen voting in a federal election is a federal crime — and knowingly facilitating such conduct is equally unlawful," warns the letter from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general at the Justice Department.

It adds: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."
The letter is addressed to the Los Angeles County Counsel's office and also is copied to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan, effectively putting the entire state on notice. Neither office immediately returned a request for comment, nor did the state attorney general.
It is unclear how many individuals the Justice Department might look to try to investigate and charge, though any federal criminal cases in the Los Angeles area would be handled by the office of Bill Essayli, the region's top federal prosecutor and one of the Justice Department officials who filed the federal complaint Thursday against California.
The Trump administration has made the pursuit of noncitizen voters a priority
Sent less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 election, the letter adds to simmering tensions over voter rolls between California and the Justice Department and reflects the Trump administration's aggressive hunt for noncitizen voters. It has made the issue a priority this year, including by demanding detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states
The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say
In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.
That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.
The letter follows a Justice Department lawsuit
The Justice Department lawsuit was filed after California officials were given, and did not meet, a 48-hour deadline to review a password-protected thumb drive that contained a list of 20,000 names. The federal government says those are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election, although the secretary of state said the administration has provided no evidence to support that claim. The state mails ballots to all registered voters.
Rick Hasen, a UCLA law professor, said the letter "ups the ante by threatening election officials with potential criminal prosecution."
"It is deplorable that rather than work cooperatively and assist states in their election administration responsibilities, the federal government is making escalating threats and unreasonable demands beyond its power in the middle of an ongoing election," he said.
Over 23 million people are registered statewide, and a handful of competitive congressional races in other California districts could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
Associated Press writers Michael R. Blood in Los Angeles and Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report.
